answer: The page does not reproduce a written board agenda as such; it gives the day's order: (1) relational databases, a brief look; (2) locking, mostly pessimistic locking, in theory then shown in a live airline check-in demo; (3) after a break, building a key-value store on top of a relational database.
evidence: Overview: 'The day is about relational databases: a brief look at them... and most of the time on locking, pessimistic locking in particular. The class ran in this order... first the theory of locking, then a live demo in which an airline check-in system is actually coded... then a short break, then a long build of a key-value store on top of a relational database.'

answer: Whenever a new, revolutionary, foundational technology comes up, its first applications are in finance (money and accounting), because society runs on money. Examples: blockchain (said to be introduced around 2012, first applications around money; the page corrects the year to 2008, Bitcoin, electronic cash), and relational databases themselves, meant for accounting (hence rows and columns); early computers' first apps were spreadsheets/ledgers.
evidence: §1.1: 'Whenever a new, revolutionary, foundational technology comes up, its first applications are in finance: money and accounting... Blockchain is the lecture's example: introduced around 2012... Relational databases fit the same pattern... accounting'; 'More precisely: ... 31 October 2008'; 'Money first' summary on ledgers.

answer: Because they were built to make financial applications possible and dealt with money: you cannot lose a transaction, what you write must be correct and never corrupted, and many people must be able to update the same data. So ACID became a core part, and the transaction became the core component of a relational database.
evidence: §1.1: 'Because they were built to make financial applications possible and dealt with money, relational databases had to give very strong guarantees. That is why ACID became a core part of them... So the transaction became the core component of a relational database.'

answer: Data is stored/represented in rows and columns; its key highlight is relations (where the name comes from) - 'you pick relational databases for relations'. They are known as the world's strictest databases (and for ACID guarantees). Formally a relation is a set of tuples (a table), linked by keys.
evidence: §1.1: 'A relational database stores and represents data in rows and columns, and its key highlight is relations... As the board put it: you pick relational databases for relations.' 'The lecture calls them the world's strictest databases.'

answer: Indexes make reads faster and writes slower: every index is one more structure each write has to update.
evidence: §1.1: 'One more property from the same board...: indexes make reads faster and writes slower. Every index is one more structure each write has to update.'

answer: Core idea: acquire the lock before you proceed. Flow: ACQ_LOCK(), then READ and UPDATE (the critical section), then REL_LOCK(); only after the release may another transaction do the same.
evidence: §1.2: 'its core idea is that you acquire the lock before you proceed'; Fig 1·a: 'The board's typical flow: ACQ_LOCK(), then READ and UPDATE, then REL_LOCK().'

answer: Two people clap at the same moment: both transactions read the same old count and both write back count + 1, so the final value is count + 1 instead of count + 2 (a lost update). count++ is read, add, write - not atomic. Locks protect the sanity of the data (consistency and integrity) against concurrent updates.
evidence: §1.2: 'Take two people clapping on a Medium story at the same moment... the final value is count + 1, not the count + 2 you expected.' 'why do we need locks? To protect the sanity of the data, its consistency and integrity, against concurrent updates.'

answer: Take a lock where the correctness of the data matters more than throughput; where correctness isn't important, it is fine to skip the lock.
evidence: §1.2 rule: 'Take a lock where the correctness of the data matters more than throughput. Where it doesn't, skip it.'

answer: T1 holds row 2 and wants (waits for) row 1, which T2 holds; T2 holds row 1 and wants row 2, which T1 holds. The waits and holds form a cycle, so nobody moves until the database rolls one back (ERROR 1213). (On the board T2 was hidden behind video tiles; per audio it is T2.)
evidence: §1.5 Fig 1·e: 'T1 holds row 2 and waits for row 1; T2 holds row 1 and waits for row 2. The two waits and the two holds form a cycle'.

answer: Check whether it can deadlock: arrange your statements and the order in which you acquire and release locks, and if a deadlock is possible, protect against it. Standard defence: every code path locks rows in the same order (e.g. ascending primary key).
evidence: §1.5: 'whenever you write code or a SQL query that takes locks, in any language, check whether it can deadlock. Arrange your statements, and the order in which you acquire and release locks... The standard defence is a single order'.

answer: Whenever a lock would make a transaction wait, the database runs deadlock detection (a cycle in the who-waits-for-whom graph). If granting the lock would create a cycle, the engine kills the transaction that fired that query, so the closing edge never forms ('the transaction that detects the deadlock kills itself'). Engine caveats: InnoDB checks at once and tries to roll back small transactions (ERROR 1213, whole txn rolled back); PostgreSQL waits deadlock_timeout (1 s) first and its victim is unpredictable; Oracle rolls back only one statement of the detecting transaction. Code must be ready to retry.
evidence: §1.5: 'Whenever a lock would make a transaction wait, the database runs a deadlock detection algorithm... the database engine kills the transaction that fired that query... The board said it as the transaction that detects the deadlock kills itself!' plus 'More precisely' note.

answer: If it entered a deadlock everything would stall and nothing would move; the only way out would be to reboot the database, meaning downtime. (Short of reboot, a lock-wait timeout or killing a session also breaks it.)
evidence: §1.5: 'If a database did enter a deadlock, everything would stall... The only way out would be to reboot the database, which means downtime, so databases never let it happen.'

answer: Start two transactions on two rows (e.g. two MySQL terminals with SET autocommit = 0 and a begun transaction) and take locks crosswise: T1 locks row 2, T2 locks row 1, then T1 asks for row 1 and T2 for row 2. When the final lock query fires, the transaction that fired it is killed.
evidence: §1.5 'See it yourself': 'Start two transactions on two rows and take the locks crosswise... the transaction that fired it is killed. §1.7 shows the two-terminal setup.' §1.7: 'open two terminals... SET autocommit = 0 and begin a transaction'.

answer: Shared locks = read locks, taken by ending a SELECT with FOR SHARE (older MySQL: LOCK IN SHARE MODE). Exclusive locks = write locks, taken with FOR UPDATE.
evidence: §1.3: 'Shared locks are also called read locks; exclusive locks are also called write locks.' 'end it with FOR SHARE'; 'To take an exclusive lock, end the SELECT with FOR UPDATE.'

answer: 1) The rows are reserved for read by the current transaction. 2) Other transactions can read the locked rows. 3) Other transactions cannot modify the locked rows. 4) If the current transaction wants to modify them, its locks are upgraded to an exclusive lock.
evidence: §1.3: 'The board listed the rules of a shared lock in four lines, in this order...'

answer: Both get their shared locks: T1 on 1,2,6 and T2 on 3,4,6, so row 6 carries two shared locks and both may read it. If T2 tries to update row 6 it must wait until T1 commits or aborts (board: T1 may read and modify; T2 may only read and wait). Page caveat: while both share row 6, T1 can't update it either; if both try, it's a deadlock and one is rolled back.
evidence: §1.3 and Fig 1·b: 'It also gets its locks, on rows 3, 4 and 6'; 'T2 has to wait until T1 commits or aborts... T1 may read and modify the row; T2 may only read and wait'; 'More precisely: ...neither can update it until the other commits or aborts'.

answer: Very high read throughput for read-only use cases: other transactions can still read the locked rows while modification is prevented.
evidence: §1.3: 'Shared locks give very high read throughput for read-only use cases: other transactions can still read the locked rows, and modification is prevented.'

answer: Its read lock is raised to an exclusive lock implicitly (automatically), and only then does the modification happen. This upgrade is a classic deadlock source if two transactions share the row and both update.
evidence: §1.3: 'its read lock is raised to an exclusive lock implicitly, without you doing anything, and only then does the modification happen. The upgrade is a classic source of deadlock'.

answer: The rows are reserved for write by the current transaction; other transactions are not even allowed to read the locked rows, let alone modify them. Caveat: in practice other transactions can't modify or lock them, but plain SELECTs still read the last committed version under MVCC (except InnoDB SERIALIZABLE with autocommit off).
evidence: §1.3: 'On the board, other transactions are not even allowed to read the locked rows, let alone modify them: the rows are reserved for write by the current transaction.' + 'More precisely' note.

answer: T2's query does not complete; it waits until T1 commits or aborts, because of row 6. If it had asked only for rows 3 and 4, its statement would have completed with rows 3 and 4.
evidence: §1.3: 'T2's query does not complete. It waits until T1 commits or aborts, because it wants row 6... Without row 6 in its set, T2's statement would have completed with rows 3 and 4.'

answer: They severely hurt throughput; but where you need exclusivity (e.g. to update a row) you have to use them.
evidence: §1.3: 'Exclusive locks severely hurt throughput. But where you need exclusivity, you have to use them.'

answer: If any rows the query wants are locked by another transaction, it skips them and proceeds best-effort with the unlocked rows instead of waiting - it removes locked rows from the result set. T2 gets rows 3 and 4 only. It gives an inconsistent view by design, meant for queue-like tables.
evidence: §1.4: 'skip them, and go ahead on a best-effort basis... it removes the locked rows from the result set.' 'T2's query for rows 3, 4 and 6 with SKIP LOCKED moves on at once and gets rows 3 and 4 only.'

answer: When you need all the rows (e.g. a specific row, like a passenger who picked seat 14C) - then you must wait. It's also not for general transactional work since it gives an inconsistent view; only for cases where any free row will do (job queues, seat pools).
evidence: §1.4: 'When you need all the rows, you have to wait; there is no other option.' 'it is not for general transactional work'; §2.6: 'You can't hand that passenger another seat, so you wouldn't use SKIP LOCKED.'

answer: If any row the query wants is locked by another transaction, the transaction kills itself / fails immediately instead of waiting. Board error: ERROR 3572: Do not wait for lock (MySQL). In MySQL only the statement errors; in PostgreSQL the whole transaction becomes aborted until ROLLBACK. Afterwards it may retry or not, depending on business.
evidence: §1.4: 'a NOWAIT locking read does not wait for the lock to be acquired; it fails immediately.' 'SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT; -- ERROR 3572: Do not wait for lock'.

answer: So you don't wait for nothing: otherwise T2 waits up to the SQL timeout (10 s in the class example), tying up that thread's share of the database and making the client wait, in a use case that doesn't care if the row is locked. Real defaults are longer: InnoDB innodb_lock_wait_timeout 50 s; PostgreSQL lock_timeout 0 = wait forever.
evidence: §1.4: 'Why have NOWAIT at all? So you don't wait for nothing. Without it, T2 waits for the lock up to the SQL query timeout, say 10 seconds...'

answer: Don't build the whole system: implement only the core you want to understand (here the database part) as small prototypes, skipping CRUD for everything else - the goal is understanding database locks, not drawing fancy boxes.
evidence: §2.1: 'It does not build the whole airline system. It builds only the part it wants to understand, the database part... implement its core, skip the CRUD for everything else, and keep the prototypes small.'

answer: Several airlines (e.g. Air India, IndiGo, Go Air); each airline has several flights; each flight has 120 seats (a deliberate oversimplification); each flight flies many trips; a passenger takes one seat on one trip of one flight. Also: it is not a reservation system - everyone has already booked and paid and only picks a seat; all 120 passengers check in at the same moment.
evidence: §2.1: 'There are several airlines, such as Air India, IndiGo and Go Air. Each airline has several flights, and each flight has 120 seats (a deliberate oversimplification). Each flight flies many trips...' 'It is not a reservation system.'

answer: airlines (id, name); flights (id, airline_id, name) pointing to airlines; trips (id, flight_id, fly_time) pointing to flights; users (id, name); seats (id, name, trip_id, user_id) pointing to its trip and the user sitting there. Each table points at the one above by id; on a new trip every user_id is NULL; the demo only writes seats.user_id.
evidence: §2.1 Fig 2·a: 'Five tables. airlines (id, name)... flights (id, airline_id, name)... trips (id, flight_id, fly_time)... users (id, name). seats (id, name, trip_id, user_id)'.

answer: Three boxes: passengers use a check-in service (end-user facing check-ins) which reads/writes seats in MySQL; an admin service (the airline's side) also writes to MySQL - it adds flights and trips, keeps them up to date, and when a trip opens for booking creates one seats row per seat with user_id NULL.
evidence: §2.1 Fig 2·b and text: 'a check-in service that passengers use, a database, and an admin service... It adds flights and trips and keeps them up to date. When a flight opens a trip for booking, it creates one row in seats for every seat... user_id set to NULL.'

answer: All 120 passengers of one flight reach the airport at the exact same moment and at 120 kiosks pick a seat at the same time - how to handle 120 people on one trip checking in simultaneously.
evidence: §2.1: 'imagine all 120 passengers of one flight reaching the airport at the exact same moment. There are 120 kiosks...' Fig 2·b footer: 'how will we handle all 120 people on one trip checking in at the same time?'

answer: Reservation/booking and payment - it's not a reservation system; passengers have already booked and paid and only pick a seat. It also doesn't build the whole airline system (no CRUD for everything, no frontend/full backend).
evidence: §2.1: 'It is not a reservation system. Everyone has already booked the flight and paid. At the kiosk they only pick a seat.' 'It does not build the whole airline system.'

answer: Go was chosen for simplicity, elegance and easy concurrency. Any language that supports concurrency works; without threads you would have to mimic 120 passengers with many processes, and threads are much easier.
evidence: §2.1 'Why Go': 'chosen for its simplicity, its elegance and its easy concurrency. Any language that supports concurrency works. Without threads you would have to mimic 120 passengers with many processes'.

answer: A sanity check: takes a user id, asks which seat to book, and books it (begin txn, SELECT seat by id, UPDATE seats SET user_id = ? WHERE id = ?, commit). Wrong: zero checks - nothing checks if the seat is already booked, so another user can book the same seat ('last one wins'), leading to two people on one seat.
evidence: §2.2: 'Approach 0 is a sanity check... There are zero checks in it. Nothing looks at whether the seat is already booked... // last one wins'.

answer: The system picks a seat at random instead of the passenger, using the same unchecked UPDATE ('overriding possible'). It fails because the random pick is from all seats, not just free ones, and random can pick the same seat in two calls, so two passengers can still get one seat.
evidence: §2.2: 'Approach 1 takes the choice away from the passenger. The system picks a seat at random... the random pick is from all the seats of the airplane, not just the free ones.'

answer: When main starts it spawns one goroutine per passenger, 120, all picking at once; each picks a random seat from all seats, starts a txn, updates, commits. Result: random didn't give 120 unique values - the seat map was mostly empty (far fewer than 120 booked) and seats 7-E and 12-E were each 'booked' by two passengers.
evidence: §2.2: 'it spawns one goroutine per passenger, 120 of them... The seat map is mostly empty, and the log has two passengers each booking seat 7-E and two more each booking 12-E.'

answer: SELECT id, name, trip_id, user_id FROM seats WHERE trip_id = 1 AND user_id IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 1; then update that seat and commit.
evidence: §2.3 query block.

answer: The transactions are concurrent: they read at the same time, before anyone has booked/committed, so the database gives all of them the same NULL seat. Without locking nothing stops transactions acting on the same old value; last write wins.
evidence: §2.3: 'the transactions are concurrent: they read at the same time, nobody has booked the seat yet, so the database gives all of them the same NULL seat. Unless some locking is in place, the same seat is offered to many passengers.'

answer: Because of ORDER BY id (LIMIT 1): every transaction sees seat 1 first (then 2, then 3), so everyone books that same seat.
evidence: §2.3: 'Which seat do they all get? The first one, and ORDER BY is the reason.'

answer: Run 1: seats 1, 2 and 3 filled; again: four seats; again: two - 2 to 4 seats, no guarantee how many, filled in seat order, with the log printing the same seat over and over (1-C, 1-C, 1-C, with 1-B and 1-A before).
evidence: §2.3: 'Seats 1, 2 and 3 filled. Run it again: four seats. Again: two. There is no guarantee how many seats get filled, they fill in seat order'.

answer: Some goroutine read, wrote and committed before a later goroutine started its read; the later reader saw seat 1's user_id no longer NULL and WHERE user_id IS NULL gave it the next row - the condition moved it, not the code or transaction. (In REPEATABLE READ, a txn sees commits that landed before its first read.)
evidence: §2.3: 'Because some goroutine ran, found the first free row, wrote to it and committed before a later goroutine started its read... It moved on because of the condition'.

answer: Line for line the same as approach 3, with two words added at the end of the SELECT: FOR UPDATE, making the read take a pessimistic exclusive lock on the row it returns.
evidence: §2.4: 'Approach 4 is approach 3, line for line, with two words added at the end of the SELECT: FOR UPDATE.'

answer: No: waiting is not deadlock. A deadlock needs a cycle - you wait on a row locked by someone who is in turn waiting on a row you hold. Here transactions merely wait.
evidence: §2.4 predictions: 'No. Waiting is not deadlock. A deadlock happens when you wait on a row locked by someone who is in turn waiting on a row you hold: it needs a cycle'.

answer: ACID holds at the level of a single transaction. Here there are concurrent transactions, and how they are scheduled depends on the isolation level ('I' comes in levels: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable). Defaults aren't serializable (MySQL repeatable read, PostgreSQL read committed), so 'read free seat then book it' can race unless you lock while reading (FOR UPDATE) or use a conditional UPDATE.
evidence: §1.6: 'ACID properties hold at the level of a transaction... how concurrent transactions are scheduled depends on the database's isolation level.' and 'Pause and think' answer.

answer: As taught, yes: under serializable transactions run one after another and you wouldn't face the seat problem - but it's pathetically slow. It isn't used for throughput and parallel writes (why should a user on row 100 wait for one on row 1). Page caveat: serializable doesn't literally queue; PostgreSQL aborts with serialization failure and you must retry, and InnoDB two bookers can deadlock - so you'd need retries.
evidence: §1.6: 'If your isolation level were serializable... Transactions would run literally one after another. That is pathetically slow, but you would not face the seat problem' + 'More precisely' + 'for practical reasons: you need high throughput and parallel writes'.

answer: The engine must treat a range query and a pointed lookup in one uniform way; a lock on a pointed row (id = 67) has no 'next row', so 'move to the next row' can't be the rule. Instead the waiter doesn't re-send anything: the engine re-evaluates the statement it's running and tries to lock what now matches.
evidence: §2.4 'You are the database engineer': 'A lock on one pointed row would never move on to the next row, so move to the next row can't be the rule.' 'the engine re-evaluates the statement it is already running'.

answer: All 120 seats filled every run (1.25 s, 1.73 s, 1.79 s on screen), in seat order (1C, 1D, 1E, 1F, 2A, 2B ...); each transaction took an exclusive lock while others waited.
evidence: §2.4: 'All 120 seats fill. Run it again: all 120. And again: all 120, every time, in 1.25 s, 1.73 s and 1.79 s on screen. The seats fill in order'.

answer: The first transaction acquires the lock on 1A; the others get no row yet (the DB returns a row only with its lock) and wait. When the holder commits/aborts, the engine signals waiters, which re-evaluate the same statement inside the engine against the new row; 1A no longer matches user_id IS NULL, so one of them locks 1B while others wait again; repeat. Waiters sleep in a wait queue, no busy loop. Worst case N(N+1)/2 evaluations (7,260 for 120).
evidence: §2.4 Fig 2·e and 'Here is the mechanism in words...'

answer: No. In the run, seat 1A went to a different user than user 1; whichever transaction gets scheduled first gets the next seat.
evidence: §2.4: 'Not user 1 seat 1, user 2 seat 2... Whichever transaction gets scheduled first gets the next seat.'

answer: Waiting and repeated work: in the worst case every waiter re-evaluates after every commit, N + (N-1) + ... = N(N+1)/2 evaluations inside the database - 7,260 for 120 - painful for the DB, and slower (~1.2-1.8 s).
evidence: §2.4: 'N + (N - 1) + ... = N(N+1)/2... For N = 120 that is 7,260. It is painful for the database to do that much work. But the system is correct.'

answer: Add SKIP LOCKED to the FOR UPDATE query. Approach 4 took ~1.7 s; approach 5 completed in 147 ms, about one tenth of the time, still filling all 120 seats.
evidence: §2.5: 'Approach 5 completed in 147 milliseconds, about one tenth of the time, and still filled all 120 seats.'

answer: The engine sees the row is locked and, because of SKIP LOCKED, moves straight on to the next row matching the WHERE clause and locks it for the second transaction (next for the third, etc.); nobody waits, rows locked back to back.
evidence: §2.5: 'the engine sees that this row is locked; because the query says SKIP LOCKED, it moves straight on to the next row that matches the WHERE clause and locks that one'.

answer: Never believe it: relational databases scale beautifully well - they can't handle big data, but at scaling and high QPS they are champions; you need performance tuning (here just normal SQL constructs); you can do partitioning, sharding, everything on them (e.g. Vitess served YouTube's MySQL traffic).
evidence: §2.5: 'relational databases scale beautifully well. They can't handle big data, but at scaling and handling high QPS they are champions.' §2.7: 'Never believe a generic statement like relational databases don't scale'.

answer: 0: passenger picks, plain UPDATE, no checks. 1: random seat from all seats, overriding possible. 2: 120 goroutines random - far fewer than 120 filled, 7-E/12-E double. 3: first free seat (IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 1) - 2-4 seats, one seat to many. 4: + FOR UPDATE - all 120, correct, 1.2-1.8 s. 5: + SKIP LOCKED - all 120 in 147 ms. Pattern: first make it fail (0-3), then correct with an exclusive lock, then SKIP LOCKED for performance - evolving by adding two or three words.
evidence: §2.5: 'First make sure the system fails (approaches 0 to 3). Then make it correct with an exclusive lock (FOR UPDATE). Then add SKIP LOCKED for performance.' + six-approach table.

answer: 'Fixed inventory + contention = locking.' Check-in: the fixed inventory is 120 seats, the contention is 120 people trying to book them, so you must take locks.
evidence: §2.7: 'Here the fixed inventory is 120 seats. The contention is 120 people... Fixed inventory + contention = locking. Remember this phrase for the rest of your life.'

answer: IRCTC: SKIP LOCKED is how you get high throughput there, so its codebase is probably full of skip locks (and exclusive locks) - an inference, not from seeing their code. BookMyShow: limited seats per screen, with an exclusive lock whoever gets it moves forward and others wait for that transaction to complete.
evidence: §2.7: 'IRCTC's code base is probably full of skip locks (and exclusive locks): an inference from the pattern... BookMyShow... With an exclusive lock, whoever gets the lock moves forward, and the others wait'.

answer: No. Locking happens in the database engine on the CPU side - a mutex doesn't let the waiting transaction proceed. Built from mutexes, semaphores, sometimes monitors, or atomic instructions, all resting on hardware atomics like test-and-set and compare-and-swap. Where the record lives differs: InnoDB keeps its lock table in memory; PostgreSQL marks row locks in the row itself (so FOR UPDATE can cause disk writes).
evidence: §1.7: 'Locking does not happen at the disk level at all. It happens in the database engine, on the CPU side: a mutex...' 'Mutexes and semaphores, and in some cases monitors...'

answer: It is not a SQL lock and no database transaction spans it - it's a 'hold'. The booking is split into phases: a momentary transaction locks the seat, sets its status to HOLD and commits; payment happens outside any transaction for ~10 minutes. A 10-minute transaction would drastically cut throughput. It's a different system, discussed with flash sale later.
evidence: §2.7 'Hold, not lock' and Fig 2·g.

answer: No - you can't hand them another seat. Use plain SELECT ... WHERE ... AND id = 67 FOR UPDATE then update. The losing transaction waits, re-evaluates the same seat, finds no rows match (or sees no rows found), and the front end shows 'seat's gone'.
evidence: §2.6: 'you wouldn't use SKIP LOCKED. You'd use the plain SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on that seat'; 'One succeeds; the other sees no rows found, or waits and then finds that no rows match, and the front end shows seat's gone.'

answer: No code needed: start a MySQL server, open two terminals, in each SET autocommit = 0 and begin a transaction, take shared/exclusive locks on the same rows and watch one session halt while the other moves (and discover deadlocks). Also code out cases like FOR SHARE then update.
evidence: §1.7 'Try it in two terminals'.

answer: No. The next transaction evaluating trip_id = 1 AND user_id IS NULL ORDER BY id matches that row again; rows are never skipped altogether; because of ORDER BY id the released row is the first the next statement picks up (even without ORDER BY it would match some free row).
evidence: §2.5: 'What if the transaction that took seat 2 fails? Seat 2 is not lost... A row is never skipped altogether.'

answer: N(N+1)/2 (7,260 for N = 120): after each commit all waiting transactions re-evaluate, one succeeds, the rest re-evaluate again: N + (N-1) + ... + 1. These are evaluations inside the database, not client queries.
evidence: §2.4: 'Without SKIP LOCKED, in the worst case all the waiting transactions re-evaluate, one succeeds, all the rest re-evaluate again... = N(N+1)/2.'

answer: The isolation level governs it - the transaction does what the isolation level says (serializable one after another; RR/RC their own behaviour). You can't write FOR UPDATE on an UPDATE. To lock explicitly, run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE first, then the UPDATE. Page note: an UPDATE itself takes an exclusive lock on rows it touches, so concurrent UPDATEs queue, and isolation level decides what the waiter does.
evidence: §1.7: 'Then the isolation level kicks in...' 'To take a lock explicitly, then, run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE first, then the UPDATE.' + 'More precisely'.

answer: There is no explicit unlock: committing (txn.Commit()) - or aborting - the transaction releases all its locks.
evidence: §1.7: 'There is no explicit unlock. Committing the transaction releases all the locks it holds, and so does aborting it.'

answer: The engine signals them: waiting threads sit in a wait queue and are signalled when the lock is released (thread signalling), then re-evaluate. Not a busy loop - they sleep until signalled.
evidence: §2.4: 'the waiters don't sit in a loop checking the lock again and again. That is what thread signalling is for: waiting threads sit in a wait queue and are signalled'.
